newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland business leaders anxious about violence.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland business leaders anxious about violence.

text.p: Northern Ireland business leaders told the British government on Monday they were worried that fresh violence would harm improved investment prospects.

Leaders of the province's "G7" business community made their views known in a meeting with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, which was scheduled before the outbreak of rioting across the province at the weekend.
The organisation, which includes representatives of the Confederation of British Industry and other key employers, said in a statement that "Northern Ireland cannot have it both ways."

"If we keep failing to get to grips with our community divisions, our economic prospects will be blighted and, sadly, the consequences will inevitably be worst for the less fortunate in our society," the statement said.
"We would urge community leaders on all sides to do everything they can to help reduce tensions," it said.

It was issued after Catholic youths inflicted millions of pounds worth of damage in overnight rioting in protest at the routing of a Protestant Orange Order parade through a Catholic area of Portadown on Sunday.
The vast majority of the damage was caused to private property, cars and security installations. There were no reports of any foreign plant coming under attack.

But G7's views reflected widespread concern in the business community that images of rioting, shooting and guerrilla violence beamed across international television networks would blemish an investment image authorities have worked to improve.

The Group called on leaders of all political parties to "renew their efforts to reach an early political accommodation and remove the uncertainty about Northern Ireland's future which is contributing to community tension," it said.
Northern Ireland's business leaders say the region has turned from an economic black spot into one of the best- performing economies in the United Kingdom in recent years.

Its image as a place for foreign investment received a boost in 1995 when U.S. President Bill Clinton launched an initiative to underpin peace hopes by holding a series of investment conferences in the United States.

Key U.S. and overseas investors went to Washington and then to Philadelphia to hear Britain's state IDB investment arm lobby them about the region's skilled, English-speaking workforce, sound infrastructure and strategic position in Europe.
But, business groups say, the drive suffered a setback when Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas fighting British rule of Northern Ireland ended a 17-month truce in February 1996.
The ending of the IRA truce has shown no immediate dropoff in investment but has done little for the province's image for investors seeking a foothold in Europe.
Last year was a record for foreign investment in Northern Ireland, which describes itself as an ideal location for electronic, hi-tech and software projects from the United States and Asia.
According to official figures, investment totalled 490 million pounds ($829 million) against 432 million in 1995/96 and 252 million in 1994/95.
G7, includes the Confederation of British Industry, hoteliers, the Institute of Directors, Chamber of Commerce and Trades Unions groups. ($ = 0.591 British Pounds)
